properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-06, extending the federation idea into his own professional domain: "in the military, when you have a clearance, there is a 'need to know' and a person only gets what they need to know. often SAP/SAR programs are like this. reflow2 could support both this mechanically by user1 being the only person to projectA... then user2 who does not have a need to know only has access to projectB... and their projectC. mechanically, they'd have to have access to some machine that could hold the graph for the different clearance levels."

NOTE ON THE EXAMPLE: Anthony flagged immediately afterwards that he had muddled which made-up project sat at which level ("oops, I think I goofed up the clearance levels of my made up projects, but hopefully the point is still valid"). It is. Nothing below rests on the specific levels — only on the SHAPE: user1 holds {A, B}, user2 holds {B, C}, and B is the overlap. The levels are deliberately not restated here, because the slip turned out to expose a real error in the first version of this node. See the correction below.

THE STRUCTURAL ANALOGY IS EXACT, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS DANGEROUS. The federation shape recorded in dec:idea-a-session-holds-several-graphs — each person holds their own subtree plus one hop outward, cuts overlapping at ownership seams — is, drawn on a whiteboard, indistinguishable from need-to-know compartmentation. The overlap graph is the shared compartment. Nothing about the picture is wrong.

⚠️⚠️ WHAT MUST NOT BE READ INTO IT, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LINE IN THIS NODE: reflow2 IS NOT AN ACCESS CONTROL AND MUST NEVER BE DESCRIBED AS ONE. It has NO AUTHENTICATION OF ANY KIND — recorded already in req:a-session-cannot-reach-another-designs-graph, and --http-allow-host is Host-header allowlisting for DNS-rebinding protection, not authentication. A list of graph_ids in a config file is a CONVENIENCE SCOPE: it says which designs a session bothers to load, not which designs a person is permitted to read. Anyone with filesystem read access to the store reads the entire design, config or no config. In most domains that distinction is pedantic. In THIS one it is the difference between a tool and an incident, and it is precisely the permission-versus-convenience question left open on the federation node — now with real consequences attached.

THE REAL SEPARATION IS THE ACCREDITATION BOUNDARY, NOT THE APPLICATION. Anthony said the mechanical part himself — "they'd have to have access to some machine that could hold the graph for the different clearance levels." The enclave, the system-high accreditation and whatever guard moves data between them are the controls. reflow2's honest role is to be COMPATIBLE with that separation, never to implement it.

⭐ AND HERE THE FEDERATION SHAPE EARNS ITS KEEP FOR A REASON THAT HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH CONVENIENCE. Because nobody holds the whole DAG — each person holds a local cut — the design CAN be split across enclaves at all. A design brain that required the whole federation resident in one process to answer a question would be unusable above unclassified, full stop. The local-cut property is what makes cross-enclave design possible, and that is an architectural argument for it independent of anything about laptops and subtrees.

⭐ THE FILE-BASED MODEL IS THE ONE THAT SURVIVES AN AIR GAP, AND IT IS NOT LEGACY. dec:multi-writer-architecture (ACCEPTED) keeps the design as a graph-in-a-repo-file with many writers merging on pull, and its product is an EXPORT — a single, complete, content-hashed, deterministic file, with a three-way merge that can reconcile two divergent copies. FILES ARE WHAT A CROSS-DOMAIN TRANSFER PROCESS CAN ACTUALLY MOVE. The hosted always-on server of dec:one-process-many-stores — flo2's model, proposed the previous day — is not that, and could not be. So reflow2 now has TWO deployment shapes serving genuinely different worlds: hosted, for flo2's non-technical browser collaborators; file-and-merge, for anything behind an accreditation boundary. Recording this because the hosted work could easily be mistaken for the direction of travel, and for this class of user the repo-file model is not the old way — it is the only way.

⚠️⚠️ THE DIRECT COLLISION WITH THE FEATURE ANTHONY ASKED FOR AN HOUR EARLIER. dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency proposes that a gap in one design automatically become a requirement in the design it depends on. IN A COMPARTMENTED SETTING, AN AUTOMATIC CROSS-GRAPH WRITE IS A CHANNEL BETWEEN COMPARTMENTS. And it is worse than the content: the mere EXISTENCE and TIMING of activity on one side can be inferable from the other — a node id, a timestamp, a counter that ticks, "someone is blocked on this" — none of which is the sensitive fact and all of which can carry it. AGGREGATION compounds it: two designs each individually releasable may not be releasable together.

⭐⭐ CORRECTION, 2026-08-06, PROMPTED BY ANTHONY'S OWN SLIP ABOUT THE LEVELS — and it changes the engineering conclusion, so it is recorded rather than quietly edited. The first version of this node said "upward may be fine, downward is spillage." THAT CONFLATED TWO DIFFERENT AXES. Dependency direction (who consumes whom) and classification direction (what is more sensitive) are INDEPENDENT, and assuming they align is exactly the mistake the muddled example accidentally surfaced.

In the example as loosely written, the most sensitive project happened to also be the most upstream, so "flows upstream" and "flows to higher classification" looked like the same sentence. THEY ARE NOT, AND REFLOW2'S OWN REAL CASE IS THE OPPOSITE ONE: dynograph-foundation is the most upstream design and the least sensitive — a public library — while its consumers are the things that could carry sensitivity. So a gap in a classified consumer flowing UP into an unclassified foundation is a flow toward LOWER classification, which is the dangerous direction. The feature's most natural and most useful direction is, in the realistic configuration, the unsafe one.

THE CONSTRAINT THEREFORE HAS TO BE STATED AGAINST THE SENSITIVITY LATTICE, NOT AGAINST THE DEPENDENCY GRAPH — "one-directional by construction" is not enough, because the design cannot know which direction is safe without being told something it currently has no vocabulary for. Which loops back to option (b) below: SOME marking axis may be unavoidable, not because reflow2 should enforce anything, but because without it the tool cannot tell the safe direction from the unsafe one and must therefore refuse to flow anything automatically at all. That is a defensible answer — refuse rather than guess is this project's standing doctrine — and it should be reached deliberately rather than by omission.

THERE IS NO MARKING VOCABULARY, AND `designation` IS NOT IT. Searched before writing: the only thing resembling a marking is `designation` on Requirements and Interfaces, whose values are `internal` / `published`. That is the SHAPE of a marking — an opt-in, per-node, computed-upon label, withheld by default and counted when withheld — but it is about PUBLICATION BOUNDARIES, not sensitivity, and reading it as a classification would be a category error. Whether reflow2 should gain a real marking axis is a schema question and therefore at least a minor version, per the CHANGELOG's own rule.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN.

(a) REFLOW2 MODELS NOTHING ABOUT CLASSIFICATION. The enclave separates; reflow2 is just a design tool that happens to run inside one. Cheapest, most honest, impossible to misread. Counter: the user still has to mark things somewhere, and it will end up in prose inside node text — the shadow-list failure again, and here an unmarked-but-sensitive statement sitting in a `statement` field is a genuine problem. AND, per the correction above, this option forecloses automatic cross-graph flow entirely, because a tool with no sensitivity vocabulary cannot know which direction is safe.

(b) A DESCRIPTIVE MARKING AXIS — a sensitivity label per node or per design, never enforcing, so an export can SAY what it contains and an automatic flow can at least refuse to run toward a lower label. Counter, and it is severe: a marking that does not enforce invites exactly the misreading warned about above, and a WRONG marking is more dangerous than none, because people act on it.

(c) REFLOW2 PROMISES ONLY NEGATIVE PROPERTIES, and says so plainly: never requires the whole federation in one place, never initiates a message (already true and verified against the service — proxy.rs), never phones home, and its export is a complete, self-describing, content-hashed file a human can inspect before it crosses anything. Marketed as COMPATIBLE WITH an accreditation boundary, never as implementing one. Cheap, truthful, and very nearly the current state already.

(d) CROSS-GRAPH FLOW IS DIRECTIONAL BY CONSTRUCTION AND EVERY CROSSING IS AN AUDITABLE EVENT — with the correction above attached: the direction must be defined against sensitivity, which (a) cannot express. Worth having on its own merits even with no classification involved, because "which design wrote into mine, when, and why" is a question any consumer wants answered.

WHAT IS NOT RECORDED HERE BECAUSE ANTHONY HAS NOT SAID IT: whether this is a real requirement he intends reflow2 to meet, or an observation that the shape happens to fit a world he knows well. He called it "just another spinoff of this idea", which reads as the latter — and the difference matters enormously, because (b) and (d) are real work and (a) and (c) are mostly writing down what is already true.
properties.name: OPEN — is the per-user graph scope a convenience or a COMPARTMENT, and what must reflow2 promise (and refuse to promise) if designs are separated by clearance?
properties.rationale:
Captured under the brainstorm skill, 2026-08-06, as the third node in one conversation — kept separate from the ACCESS question (dec:idea-a-session-holds-several-graphs) and the AUTHORITY question (dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency) because it asks a third thing: what reflow2 may TRUTHFULLY CLAIM about separation, which is a question about the product's promises rather than about its mechanism.

CORRECTED WITHIN THE HOUR, AND THE CORRECTION IS KEPT IN THE NODE rather than silently replacing the text — the same discipline dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs used on 2026-08-05, and for the same reason: the failure mode should stay visible. The first version asserted "upward may be fine, downward is spillage", which quietly assumed the dependency ordering and the sensitivity ordering run together. They do not, and reflow2's own dependency chain is a counterexample — dynograph-foundation is simultaneously the most upstream and the least sensitive design in it. The error surfaced only because Anthony flagged that he had muddled the levels in his own example, which forced a re-read; a tidier example would have hidden it. Recorded as chg:classification-and-dependency-are-orthogonal.

Written with a deliberate bias toward what reflow2 must NOT say. Anthony is a Space Force systems engineer and this is his working domain, so the failure mode here is not that reflow2 lacks a feature — it is that a structural resemblance between "per-user graph scoping" and "need-to-know" gets read as a security property by someone who then relies on it. The node therefore leads with the disclaimer rather than the opportunity, and the disclaimer is drawn from intent the design already holds rather than from caution: req:a-session-cannot-reach-another-designs-graph states in its own text that reflow2 has no authentication and that authorization belongs to the layer in front.

Also recorded because it re-values something that could otherwise look superseded: the repo-file-plus-merge model (dec:multi-writer-architecture, accepted) is the ONLY one of reflow2's two deployment shapes that can cross an air gap, since its product is a complete deterministic file and a three-way merge. The hosted multi-graph work of the previous day is additive, not a migration, and this is the clearest statement yet of who each shape is for.
